title: Observability Never Really Shifted Left
summary: We shifted testing, security, and CI/CD left. Observability stayed in production. With AI writing code faster, validation is the bottleneck.
body_markdown:
We made software development faster. Now we need to make validation faster, too.


For the last decade we have shifted development left. Testing, security, performance, and CI/CD all moved closer to the developer. Observability mostly did not. It still starts after deployment (we covered the incident side of this in[Your Observability Stack Found the Fire](https://speedscale.com/blog/your-observability-stack-found-the-fire/) ), which means the people writing the code rarely have meaningful production behavior to observe while they build.


🎯 Key Takeaways


- Testing, security scanning, and CI/CD moved left. Observability still starts after deployment, so developers have nothing real to observe while coding.
- Developers don’t ignore observability because they dislike it. A laptop or dev cluster has no customer traffic, production dependencies, or production-scale behavior to look at.
- AI shrank coding time and stretched validation time. The fix is to capture real production behavior and replay it in development before the change ships.


Alan Mon walks through the argument in 36 seconds:


## We shifted everything left except observability


A developer can run unit tests, security scans, and performance checks from a laptop or a development cluster. Observability is different. It is designed around what happens in production, and developers are expected to learn from production telemetry even though they are not running production workloads where they write code.


```text
flowchart LR
subgraph Left["Moved left"]
A[Unit tests] --> B[Security scans]
B --> C[Performance checks]
C --> D[CI/CD]
end
subgraph Right["Still on the right"]
E[Production telemetry]
end
D --> F[Deploy]
F --> E


```


## Why developers don’t use observability


It is easy to say developers don’t use observability. The reality is simpler: there is often nothing meaningful to observe.


A laptop or dev cluster has no real customer traffic, no production dependencies, and no production-scale behavior. You can’t run production traffic through a developer’s laptop and expect the same signals. Developers don’t need another dashboard. They need realistic application behavior they can work with.


## AI shortened coding time and expanded validation time


AI is changing the economics of software development. Code that once took hours can now be generated in minutes, or seconds. That creates a new bottleneck: validation.


We are producing code faster than ever while the time and effort needed to decide whether that code works can grow. The answer is to keep coding fast and move testing and observability earlier in the development cycle.


## Bring production behavior left


Observability can’t truly shift left unless the data shifts left with it. Capture real production behavior as production context, replay it safely in development, observe the results, and use that feedback to validate changes before they reach production.


```text
flowchart LR
A[Production traffic] -->|capture| B[Recorded requests and responses]
B -->|replay| C[Dev environment or laptop]
C -->|observe| D[Validation results]
D -->|fix and repeat| C
D -->|confident change| E[Ship]


```


The goal is to give developers realistic behavior they can use to build and validate with confidence, without recreating all of production on a laptop. With[proxymock](https://speedscale.com/proxymock/) , that means recording traffic once and replaying it against your service, with its dependencies mocked, every time you change the code.


## Try it with proxymock


Here is the smallest version of this loop. Install` proxymock` (see the[installation guide](https://docs.speedscale.com/proxymock/getting-started/installation/) ), then record your service while you or your tests exercise it. Replace the last argument with however you start your app:


```text
proxymock   record   --app-port   8080   --   ./mvnw   spring-boot:run
```


Stop the recording and the requests and responses are saved as files in your repo. After you change code, replay that traffic against the new build and see what differs:


```text
proxymock   replay   --in-dir   ./proxymock/recorded   --test-against   http://localhost:8080
```


To work without live dependencies, serve the recorded downstream responses from a mock instead:


```text
proxymock   mock   --in-dir   ./proxymock/recorded
```


The[quickstart](https://docs.speedscale.com/proxymock/getting-started/quickstart/) walks through the full flow.


LLM prompt for this step


```text
Check installed proxymock help for the supported recording-directory flag, then record the Maven-started Spring Boot app on port 8080. Stop cleanly, run the app with explicit recorded dependencies and no passthrough, replay the inbound requests to the actual listener, and inspect the resulting verdict.
```


## The bottom line


AI has made writing code faster. Now we need to make validation faster. That means bringing observability and testing into the development cycle, instead of waiting for production to tell us whether the code works.


Stop finding bugs in production. Catch them before they ship.


## Run this workflow with an LLM


Give this prompt to a coding assistant with access to your project and this article. Supply environment-specific values it cannot discover.


Whole-workflow LLM prompt


```text
Read https://speedscale.com/blog/observability-never-really-shifted-left/ and inspect my project instructions first. Record representative requests and outbound calls for my local Spring Boot app, rerun with recorded dependencies, and replay inbound requests against the candidate. Preserve the original recording and report semantic mismatches and test evidence alongside telemetry. Check installed tool help before adapting commands. Report the checks actually run, their results, and anything you could not verify.
```
